highlights.title: Rural Data Centers Are in for a Big Federal Tax Break
highlights.summary: Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, data center projects in rural areas could be eligible for major tax benefits starting next year. Some hyperscalers do not seem eager to take the free cash.
body: Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
On January 1, a new tax windfall will kick in that could benefit scores of rural data center projects—all thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Starting next year, projects sited in tracts of rural land across the country will be newly eligible for a set of specific corporate tax benefits under a program expanded by the bill. The new rules “may significantly lower barriers for large-scale, capital-intensive projects in rural areas—most notably hyperscale data centers,” said a statement from Ways and Means Committee chair Jason Smith last year. “The economic case for building data centers in designated rural opportunity zones becomes far more compelling” with the new program, he continued.
But experts warn that the results for rural communities could be mixed.
points: Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, data center projects in rural areas could be eligible for major tax benefits starting next year.

highlights.title: Daryz seeks historic Arc double
highlights.summary: Daryz seeks to retain his Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe crown in the 2026 renewal of Europe's richest race - live on Sky Sports Racing at 3.05pm.
body: Daryz - last year's Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe winner - looks to become the first colt to retain the prize since 1978 when he goes to post for Europe's premier race at 3.05pm, live on Sky Sports Racing; The race is the feature of eight from Paris, alongside domestic racing from Uttoxeter.
Daryz will look for an historic back-to-back double in Europe's biggest race, bidding to be the first colt since Alleged in 1978 to achieve this feat.

Francis-Henri Graffard's colt looked as good as ever when he returned in the Prix Ganay, which was then followed up with an equally sparkling performance in the Prix Aga Khan IV. A trip to Royal Ascot in June for the Prince Of Wales' Stakes didn't go to plan as he was third, although it transpired blood issues were found following the race.

After a break, Graffard's star made light work of Coronation Cup winner Bay City Roller - who he reopposes today - in the Prix Foy, with the trainer saying he was only 75 per cent fit. Having been drawn in stall five, this short priced favourite will take all the beating with connections very confident.

highlights.title: The Nvidia Shield TV Is 7 Years Old. It Just Got a $100 Price Hike
highlights.summary: The price of anything with memory is skyrocketing thanks to AI. Aging streaming devices are no exception.
body: The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.

The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.

Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.

highlights.title: GOTY 2026’s Final Nomination Is a Battleground of 8/10 Games
highlights.summary: One rung below this level, though — alright, maybe two rungs below, after the likes of Resident Evil Requiem and Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave — exists a mass of big games that were solid, impressive, and roundly satisfying, all of which got good-but-maybe-not-great reviews from critics.
body: Has 2026 been a vintage year for games? Arguably not. There's been plenty of good stuff to play, there always is. But, at this late stage in the year, we've yet to see any games that rise above and make a bid for modern classic status. There's been no Clair Obscur, no Baldur's Gate 3. And average review scores, across the board, are down. At present, only three new games — not remakes or reissues or expansions — have attained the magic 90-plus rating on review aggregation site Metacritic.
007 First Light. Gears of War: E-Day. Star Wars: Zero Company. Pragmata. Saros. Onimusha: Way of the Sword. Nioh 3. Control Resonant. The Blood of Dawnwalker.

highlights.title: Supercell, Rovio, Playdemic, First Touch, Sybo and more back SpecialEffect’s One Special Day
highlights.summary: Many major mobile game makers are giving a percentage of their UK revenue to disability charity Special Effect today, Friday October 2. Partners taking part in the One Special Day promotion include Supercell, Rovio, Sybo, Playdemic, Fingersoft, Supersolid, Hyper Luminal Games, New Star Games…
body: A slice of player spend from games including Clash of Clans, Brawl Stars, Clash Royale, Angry Birds 2, Golf Clash, Subway Surfers, Dream League Soccer, 8 Ball Pool and more will be donated to Special Effect for today only. A full list of participating games is available via the One Special Day site.

Special Effect provides assessments and customised technology loans to help physically disabled people play games, and takes what it learns back to hardware and software developers to help make their products more accessible. Thousands of disabled people ask for the charity’s help every year.

“We’ve been proud to partner with Special Effect across our games for nearly a decade, and that relationship has grown far beyond One Special Day,” said Supercell’s Deborah Mensah-Bonsu. “From cycling in Helsinki and joining One Special Walk in London, to learning from their incredible work as we think more deeply about inclusive design, we’re continually inspired by their tenacity, generosity and tremendous heart, and by how they show the games industry can genuinely change lives for the better.”

highlights.title: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon
highlights.summary: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand? I must admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena.
body: John Cena is a company man. The word “loyalty” comes up often, and about everything from his friends back home to the wrestling to the US itself. Admirable, no doubt. But Cena’s loyalty has drawn him into some uncomfortable positions, and for 20 minutes our good-natured chat about reliability, discipline and what it means to owe everything to something bigger than yourself has set us on a collision course with one of the most disgraced figures in modern entertainment.

Cena was born in West Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1977, one of five boys in a household that watched every dollar. His grandma and grandpa lived in an adjoining house. “There was a lot of ‘How are we going to pay the bills, how are we going to keep the lights on?’” Cena says. He worshipped the movie action men of the era – Schwarzenegger, Stallone, Willis – but he also loved hip-hop, which in suburban Massachusetts made him a target for bullies. Bodybuilding was the answer, and it doubles as an origin story – the boy bullied for dressing like a white rapper, growing up to become an icon for the next generation of suburban youth.

highlights.title: Keurig Alta First-Look: No More Plastic K-Cups
highlights.summary: Keurig is ready to ditch the K-Cup with a compostable and plastic- and aluminum-free coffee pod, but the price is steep.
body: Opinions on Keurig’s K-Cup System fall into two camps: fans who value the convenience of a quick java hit and coffee purists who sideline it as flavored water. I land somewhere in the middle: I grind my own beans and brew them through a reusable filter, but I let the machine do the rest. So, perhaps, I’m the customer that Keurig has in mind with its new Alta system.

The Alta is Keurig's first single-serve coffee maker that uses plastic- and aluminum-free coffee pods—finally launching after years of development. If Alta takes off, we are likely seeing the beginning of the end for the disposable K-Cup, which launched in 1998.

Whatever your thoughts are on how the perfect cup should be made, for nearly 50 million homes in the US (and not counting the many more in offices), Keurig is coffee. For almost 30 years, we’ve been trained to ditch the old drip-coffee maker for disposable single-serve pods. But now, Keurig wants us to leave (eventually) the K-Cup and embrace the AltaRounds pod, a compostable, compressed coffee round that works the same: Drop it into the machine, press a button or two, and out comes joe.

highlights.title: This is how we do it: ‘My mistress has complete control over me and makes me so happy’
highlights.summary: LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix – and it has been a revelation for them both. • How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously. I have cerebral palsy and live with my parents. Lady Alice is a delicious secret.
body: I met Lady Alice on X. We aren’t lovers or friends. She is my mistress and has complete control over me. I am hers to use however she pleases and she expects nothing less than absolute obedience. I don’t pay Lady Alice a fee, though I might pay for a service she needs such as a pedicure. These payments are “tributes”, tokens of respect and devotion.
I am 43 and use a wheelchair because I have cerebral palsy. I live with my elderly parents; they cut up my food and wash me. Lady Alice is a precious secret.

I never felt in control and hated my body. I had sexual impulses, but because I have ornamental hips that I can’t thrust and erectile dysfunction, I’m not equipped for sex in the conventional sense. I had a “friend with benefits” 20 years ago. We had two – admittedly fun – meetings that unfortunately lacked any real penetration.

In our sessions she makes me feel like there’s nothing wrong with me, as though I was simply born to kneel and be her “stress toy”. I need help cutting up food due to limited control over my fingers, but I am able to crawl and get down on my knees for Lady Alice.

Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers.

highlights.title: Humphries to face Price in World Grand Prix final in 2023 repeat
highlights.summary: Gerwyn Price and Luke Humphries will look for their second World Grand Prix titles when they meet in Sunday's final of the double-start event in Leicester.
body: Price, the 2020 champion, beat Nathan Aspinall 5-2 in Saturday's first semi-final before 2023 winner Luke Humphries defeated James Wade 5-3 to reach his fourth straight final and set up a repeat of the showpiece game three years ago - when he saw off Price 5-2.

A major drought will end either way at the Mattioli Arena, with Humphries going over a year since his last premier title - the 2025 Premier League - and Price's previous elite silverware coming way back in 2022 at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
Price romped into a 3-0 lead over Aspinall, peeling off two 13-darters and then a 15-darter to sweep the opener before he broke The Asp in the deciding leg of set two.
The third set went on throw until the fourth leg, when Aspinall missed six darts to hold, including two at double one, and Price subsequently pinned D10 to move 3-0 up.

highlights.title: Nivalis Nights dares to ask what if Cyberpunk 2077 met Dave the Diver and Stardew Valley? And for now at least I'm loving the answer
highlights.summary: As I throw open the windows on my first day in Nivalis, breathing in the city's neon-streaked air and watching the smog roil across the blackened sky, my government-mandated AI automata informs me the district is in lockdown and a serial killer's on the loose.
body: It is, though, kind of fascinating as it starts from a familiar point and begins building outward. It's also, for context, the follow-up to developer Ion Lands' enjoyable neo-noir delivery adventure Cloudpunk, taking that game's stylish dystopia and reimagining it as the setting for a sort of mash-up of Cyberpunk 2077, Stardew Valley, and Dave the Diver. It's an odd mix, certainly, but it works.

A lot of its early success is down to Nivalis itself. Cloudpunk's city was mostly designed to be viewed from afar, but Nivalis Nights plays out in first-person, demanding a world that can withstand closer scrutiny. And Ion Lands more than rises to the challenge. This Nivalis might still be a world built from jagged pixel-art edges, but it's a richly detailed, wonderfully evocative one (stubbornly wonky framerate aside); a chance to live your own little Blade Runner life, right down to the Vangelis-inspired soundtrack.

highlights.title: The hidden daytime dance revolution - and the man who captured it on camera
highlights.summary: Tim Smith's shots of the early 'daytimers' bhangra scene in Bradford feature in a Tate exhibition.
body: For decades, photographer Tim Smith's images of Bradford's British Asian "daytimers" dance scene remained largely unseen. Now, some of those shots are taking their place in a major Tate exhibition examining the creativity and rebellion that transformed 1990s Britain.
On a bright afternoon in Bradford, shoppers moved through the city centre carrying bags, going about their day.
Behind a nearby doorway, another side of Bradford was pulsing to a very different rhythm.
Tim Smith remembers stepping out of a small nightclub beneath the Alhambra theatre after spending hours photographing a "daytimers" disco.

highlights.title: Elusive ‘Geoneutrinos’ Are Building a New Map of Earth’s Volatile Interior
highlights.summary: A global network of detectors are reporting some of the most substantial measurements yet of neutrinos created deep underground by the radioactive elements that power our planet’s tectonic activity.
body: In a laboratory 2 kilometers underground, a crane lowers Matt Depatie, a detector technologist, through a hatch into a white-walled cavern filled with about 7,000 tons of ultrapure water that glows as blue as wiper fluid in the light. “Splashdown,” Depatie says over a radio as he steps into an inflatable raft waiting below.

Normally, the cavern is one of the darkest places on Earth, but today it is lit up for maintenance, offering us a rare chance to see inside. I peer through the hatch at Depatie as he paddles over to examine the submerged experiment. He’s inspecting a house-sized detector built to catch some of the most elusive particles known to physics: neutrinos.

This is the SNO+ neutrino experiment, buried deep within the Creighton mine at Snolab, an underground physics laboratory in Sudbury, Canada. SNO+ consists of an acrylic sphere lined with nearly 10,000 sensitive light detectors and filled with 780 tons of oily liquid scintillator, which flashes when lit up by energetic particles. The water around the device and the rock above it shield the detector from the glare of cosmic radiation, allowing the flickers of less common particle interactions to shine through.
points: A global network of detectors are reporting some of the most substantial measurements yet of neutrinos created deep underground by the radioactive elements that power our planet’s tectonic activity.

body: The head coach insisted there was no extra pressure after drawing a blank in their opening two Nations League games, but he and the players silenced some critics with a strong performance in Skopje despite a second red card inside a week as they beat North Macedonia 2-0.

Robertson missed two brilliant chances before Kieron Bowie - hooked after Jack Hendry's early sending off against Switzerland in midweek - smashed the ball into the bottom corner to earn his first international goal and Scotland's first in over 420 minutes.
Play was stopped by a dog running onto the pitch before Scotland continued to dominate with Bowie, Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak going close before the break.
Scotland were awarded a penalty when Gannon-Doak went down in the box after half-time, only for the referee to overturn his decision after being called to the monitor.

highlights.title: Muse Creates Detailed Profiles of All Your Friends and Family
highlights.summary: Millions have downloaded Meta’s AI agent Muse. But getting it to do your bidding comes with privacy costs.
body: Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.

In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.

Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.

highlights.title: 65 Years Ago, The Twilight Zone Aired Its Creepiest Episode
highlights.summary: The Twilight Zone ’s terror successfully bypassed television censorship of the 1960s with speculative fiction. Over five seasons, Serling, as host and writer, examined science, superstition, prejudice, and identity.
body: Horror that doesn’t reside in literal liminal spaces manifests in surreal realities. This transitional space, known as the “twilight zone,” doesn’t adhere to the rules of human society. Rod Serling knew it well. His acclaimed horror anthology series explored stories that were disturbing and unusual, often ending with a twist and a moral lesson.

“His name is Anthony Fremont. He's six years old with a cute little-boy face and blue guileless eyes. But when those eyes look at you, you'd better start thinking happy thoughts. Because the mind behind them is absolutely in charge. This is the Twilight Zone.”

Anthony (Billy Mumy) has used his god-like mental powers to create a tyrannical society with no true sense of freedom. Anthony is not doing anything out of malice. He has never been disciplined by his parents, which is why he is clueless about morality and its consequences.

highlights.title: Alone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’
highlights.summary: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife.
body: A s photographed at night from a satellite, or the International Space Station (ISS), the Iberian peninsula looks encrusted with lights along its coastal edges. Madrid forms a big pulsing cluster near the centre, while surrounding hinterlands appear as something of a void. Ever fewer people live out in Castile and León and Extremadura, adjoining regions that cover much of what is known as La España Vac ía, or “Empty Spain”.

Not many visit either, or at least not compared with Barcelona and other glowing nodes of the tourist circuit. So, while the big ports and resorts struggle to manage surplus holidaymakers, there is room for plenty more out west, toward the Portuguese border. Some have been following the stars that way lately, under the auspices of an astrotourism initiative called Extremadura Buenas Noches.

A route map plotted point-to-point between optimal stargazing sites leads to distant outposts like La Siberia (so-called because it felt that remote to workers who laid down the first roads and railways in these parts) and the Corral de los Lobos, an ancient stone enclosure on a hilltop, built to trap wolves when they outnumbered the farmers and shepherds around here.
points: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife.

highlights.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
highlights.summary: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology. A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
body: David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.

Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.

Writing in the Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”
Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”
points: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology.

body: An exceptional story arc can elevate even a flawed anime series. Although the mechanics of a great arc vary, the best tend to raise the stakes, test their characters, and build steadily toward a cathartic payoff. The conflict must also feel convincing, with the antagonist’s evolving goals and the heroes’ shifting motivations driving the story forward.

Perfection is subjective, but the finest anime arcs share a few qualities: They’re memorable, well-paced, emotionally compelling, and resolved in a meaningful way. With those standards in mind, these five story arcs come remarkably close to perfection. We wouldn’t change a thing.
What happens when a brilliant story ends with an equally brilliant final arc?

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is filled with memorable stretches, from its exploration of the Ishvalan War to the heroes’ hunt for the Homunculi. But the anime saves its best for last with the Promised Day arc, a chaotic culmination of Father’s 400-year plan for Amestris and the intertwined destinies of Edward and Alphonse Elric.

highlights.title: My friends are spouting conspiracy theories – what should I say? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
highlights.summary: You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own. Recently, I had a conversation with a friend who explained that her ill health was down to reasons I would describe as dubious. Taking certain supplements and changing her diet have significantly improved her health.
body: I’ve got another friend who thinks cholesterol is a lie and that we should live largely on meat (and supplements). Another went through a sugar causes cancer phase. And another is s ceptical of vaccines. Each of them may be right. They might not. We are learning more about the human body every day. But I was raised by scientists and I want to see a large-scale trial before I get outraged and change the way I live. Equally, I’m not convinced that a lightly regulated for-profit industry (supplements) is automatically more trustworthy than a highly regulated for-profit one (pharma).

I want to be respectful of their choices and the research they have done into their specific conditions, but for them to respect my beliefs too. The feeling I get is that they think they have the keys to the real intel and I’m being duped by the medical establishment. Or that I’m not a good friend because I don’t believe them.

I’m not sure how to have a respectful conversation about that. I ’d prefer to avoid it, but it comes up often. I find myself making non-committal comments such as “how interesting”. But I know, and they know, I’m sceptical.
points: You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own.

body: Soviet sci-fi pushed the boundaries of the genre long before its amplification during the Space Race. One of the most enduring Soviet silent classics is about space travel: Yakov Protazanov’s Aelita (1924), which explores the mundane realities of post-civil war Moscow while championing early sci-fi elements. Aelita, however, was released during an age of radical experimentation, which would soon come to an end due to heavy state censorship until the late 1950s. Although censorship was comparatively lax throughout the ‘60s and ‘70s, any overt political dissent or unorthodox filmmaking was met with pushback.

highlights.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
highlights.summary: Associate Professor Cathy Wu uses reinforcement learning to help map out improvements to transportation and other multifaceted systems.
body: As far back as she can remember, Cathy Wu ’12, MNG ’13 wanted to find ways to solve problems to improve people’s lives. Her parents were Taiwanese immigrants, and her father had a long commute to his job, which took him away from the family. On a tight budget, the rest of the family often stayed home on a street that was too busy for playing outdoors. Wu and her siblings ended up playing a lot of computer games.

Wu says her desire to make the world a better place, her dad’s daily battle against traffic, and the games she played, like “SimCity,” were the seeds of her motivation to design safe, efficient transportation systems.

Wu is an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Her research focuses on using machine learning and reinforcement learning (RL) to advance reliable strategies for improving a range of complex systems, including transportation.

points: Shortly after we were robbed in San Francisco earlier this year, we happened across a hacker and maker space known as Noisebridge.
The space is open to the public, maintained as a non-profit working space, and has tools and teaching for 3D printing, laser cutters, CNCs, woodshop tools, knitting and…
We learned about meshnet and meshcore decentralized networking, hacking hardware, and just doing cool things with technology while visiting.
Visit Noisebridge at 272 Capp St, San Francisco, CA 94110.
